findings.title: New abstract order() method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: CryptoProvider is a public extension interface, but order() is added as an abstract method. Every existing implementation outside the three updated in this PR (custom server providers, downstream/client-repo implementations, mocks and test doubles) will fail to compile until it adds order(). This is an avoidable source/binary contract break for an ordering feature: order() should be a default method with a documented default priority, with built-in providers overriding it as needed.

findings.title: Equal-order providers are silently and nondeterministically selected instead of rejected
findings.body: detectProvider() sorts by order() descending and unconditionally returns the first provider. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so when more than one is on the classpath the winner depends on ServiceLoader encounter/classpath order. Previously this configuration failed fast with 'Multiple crypto providers loaded'; now Keycloak can silently run with DefaultCryptoProvider instead of the FIPS provider (or vice versa), defeating an operator's explicit FIPS configuration and hiding a misconfiguration. Ties for the highest order should remain an error, or the mutually exclusive full providers need distinct, intentional priorities.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns an arbitrary non-BouncyCastle provider
findings.body: The CryptoProvider contract states getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the (FIPS or non-FIPS) BouncyCastle provider, but this implementation returns the provider of the JVM default KeyStore type (typically SUN/SunJSSE for PKCS12). Any caller that uses the returned provider for BC-only algorithms, keystore types or provider-name assumptions will get NoSuchAlgorithm/NoSuchProvider failures or silently different crypto behaviour. Like WildFlyElytronProvider, it should return null if no BC provider exists, or throw UnsupportedOperationException, rather than misidentify an unrelated JCA provider as BouncyCastle.

findings.title: ECDSA test never verifies the produced DER signature and does not test provider ordering
findings.body: test() only checks DER->RS->DER->RS self-consistency using the same custom ASN.1 encoder/decoder pair, and generates a single default EC key pair regardless of whether ES256, ES384 or ES512 is under test. A mutually compensating encoder/decoder defect, or DER that JCA rejects, would still pass, and the central new behaviour of this PR (CryptoIntegration choosing between AuthzClientCryptoProvider order 100 and a full provider order 200, including tie handling) has no test at all. The test should verify asn1Des with Signature.verify() using a curve-appropriate key pair, and CryptoIntegration selection should be covered directly.
